overview: Ibadan grew from an 1829 military settlement into a powerful Yoruba city-state led by warrior chiefs. The imported 1878 to 1914 interval continues beyond the start of British rule in 1893.

periods.title: A military city takes shape
periods.summary: Migrants from several Yoruba communities built the new settlement and its military power.

periods.title: Regional dominance and prolonged warfare
periods.summary: Ibadan expanded its influence, while warfare endangered farms and strained diplomacy.

periods.title: Colonial rule and a continuing city
periods.summary: British control ended political independence; Ibadan’s social and intellectual life continued.

sections.title: War, power and the costs of expansion

items.text: Ibadan’s nineteenth-century rulers were a military oligarchy: powerful chiefs, rather than an oba with an inherited royal position. The city attracted ambitious newcomers, but warfare also brought captives, destruction and insecurity to the surrounding country.

The early population included people from Ife, Oyo and Ijebu, living in different districts. Oyo leaders eventually prevailed. Ibadan’s army defeated forces from Ilorin at Osogbo around 1840, helping check their further advance and increasing the new city’s regional strength.

During the later wars, raiders threatened the farms that fed Ibadan. Samuel Johnson describes forts placed along vulnerable routes and hunters watching for attackers while cultivators worked. An army needed food, and protecting a farmer could matter as much as guarding a town gate.

The Kiriji settlement of 1886 did not instantly bring peace everywhere. Johnson describes further appeals, messengers and negotiations over the continuing Ibadan-Ilorin conflict. Ending a long war required agreements to be carried out in scattered camps, not simply a document signed in one place.

A later architectural study describes the older compound model: rooms facing one or more courtyards, with covered verandas used for household work and cooking. These spaces put cooking, conversation and visiting close together. The researcher’s fieldwork was in the late 1960s, documenting a changing inheritance.

In that compound model, the household head received visitors opposite the entrance, while guests, clients and more distant relatives often occupied rooms nearer the gate. The layout expressed social relationships. The study also emphasizes that only a few examples of this older form then survived.

Anna Hinderer’s mission school began with a handful of children in 1853. Attendance depended on family choices: parents withdrew Adelotan and Abudu while she was away in 1854. School history therefore includes negotiations within households, not just the decisions of missionaries.

Hinderer’s account describes stories, singing and a playgroup for the first pupils. When offered lessons while living at home, children wanted to continue coming. This is a particular mission classroom, remembered through its teacher’s letters, rather than a picture of every child’s education.

sections.title: Remembering relatives and making new things

items.text: Nineteenth-century records describe relatives buried within household buildings and mourners gathering for music and meals. Such practices kept ancestors connected with family space. The arrival of church graveyards raised a serious question for converts: where would they belong after death?

Church burial created work for carpenters making coffins. Adeboye names James Okuseinde, Jacob Oja and F. L. Akiele among the early Christian craftsmen. Changes in religion could therefore reshape a workshop’s orders as well as the ceremonies held around a grave.

A small Yoruba writing sample is “Iwe Itan Ibadan”, meaning “History of Ibadan”, the title of Isaac Babalola Akinyele’s 1911 book as cited by historians. It grew from a public lecture requested by a local society. Residents were organizing, discussing and publishing their own past.

Ibadan’s later intellectual life included the university founded in 1948. Its first students began in buildings previously used as a military hospital; the chiefs and people provided land for a permanent site. A city associated with military power became an important place for medicine, science and learning.

ending.text: British rule ended Ibadan’s independence in 1893. The map’s 1914 endpoint is a colonial cutoff. Families and institutions endured, and the city became a major educational center within Nigeria.
